problemText: An allusion is a reference to another story, myth, or well-known event that a writer uses in just a few words or a name. When you read an allusion, what does it bring into the sentence from the source story?
choices: A comparison using the words 'like' or 'as' to show how one thing is similar to another thing
All of the details from the source story, including every character, setting, and event that occurred in the original tale
A definition or explanation of an unfamiliar word so that the reader is able to understand the meaning of the sentence
One or two specific parts of the source story that match what is happening in the excerpt
hints: An allusion brings in only the part of the source story that fits the writer's purpose—not the whole tale.
For example, a reference to the Trojan horse brings in the idea of hidden harm that looks like a gift, not every detail about the wood, the Greek soldiers, and the city gates.

problemText: Read this sentence: 'When Marcus stepped up to perform his piano solo, he felt like Prometheus stealing fire from the gods.' (In the Greek myth, Prometheus stole fire from the gods to give humans a power they were not supposed to have, and was punished severely for it.) Which part of the Prometheus story does the allusion import in this sentence?
choices: That Marcus is doing something he knows is dangerous or forbidden, risking consequences to show courage
That Marcus will face a severe punishment from an authority figure after his performance is finished
That Marcus has trained for years and loves music more than any other activity or interest
That Marcus is taking something valuable that belongs to someone else and trying to hide it from them
hints: Ask which part of the Prometheus source matches Marcus's situation with a piano solo — not all of the myth.
The test is: what part of stealing fire fits what is actually happening here?

problemText: A writer has two choices for this moment: write 'The small mistake felt huge and changed everything,' or use an allusion to Pandora's Box (the myth where Pandora opens a box she was warned not to open, and every evil and misfortune in the world spills out, and nothing can be put back). Why would the writer choose the allusion instead of the plain sentence?
choices: The allusion is shorter and uses fewer words than the plain sentence
The allusion carries that one small action cannot be undone and releases consequences no one can control
The allusion explains that opening the box was an accident, not on purpose
The allusion tells the reader exactly what kind of mistake was made and how many people noticed
hints: What does Pandora's Box import that the plain sentence 'the mistake felt huge and changed everything' loses?
The three-part answer asks why the writer reached for it — what did the borrowed story carry that the plain one drops?

problemText: Read this excerpt: 'Every time Zoe tried a new sport, she was Icarus. She joined the swim team and nearly drowned in the first lap. She signed up for rock climbing and got stuck halfway up the wall. She tried soccer and kicked the ball into her own goal.' (Icarus ignored his father's warning not to fly too close to the sun, flew too high anyway, and fell when the wax melted.) What does the repeated allusion import about Zoe, and what does it do to the tone?
choices: It imports that Zoe is a mythical figure who does not exist in real life, and the tone is angry and bitter because she experiences failure repeatedly
It imports that Zoe is brave and heroic like the original Icarus, and the tone is admiring and serious because she is trying to accomplish great things
It imports that Zoe ignores warnings and pushes too hard, and the tone is wry and self-mocking because a city's fall is being set beside comical sports disasters
It imports that Zoe is incapable of learning from her mistakes and never improves, and the tone is sad and sympathetic because nothing she attempts ever works out
hints: Which part of Icarus fits Zoe's behavior — what does the myth import into these sentences?
The size test: a boy falling from the sky is huge; a swimmer nearly drowning in the first lap and a soccer own-goal are small. What tone does that gap create?

problemText: Read this extended analogy: 'The argument was a tennis match. Keiko served first with her main point. James returned it with a counter-argument. Keiko hit it back with new evidence. James stood at the net and called it out, and the rally ended.' Map the parts of the analogy and explain what it imports about the argument that a plain sentence could not carry.
choices: It imports that the argument had multiple exchanges in which each person tried to win by pressing their point, showing power and control in a way that plain words like 'we went back and forth' cannot fully capture
It imports that Keiko had superior debating skills and deserved to speak first because she demonstrated greater knowledge and confidence than James throughout their discussion
It imports that Keiko and James were competing for dominance and enjoying the intellectual challenge, so they continued the exchange until one person conceded defeat and agreed with the other
It imports that each person was trying to win and hit the point past the other, and that James got the final word and stopped the exchange before Keiko could respond
hints: Map each part: what is Keiko, what is James, what is the rally, what is James calling it out at the net?
What does the tennis analogy show about who had power and who stopped the conversation — and what does the plain sentence 'we argued' drop?

problemText: Read this passage: 'Our group was a ship in a storm. I was at the helm, trying to steer us through. Cameron and Lily were below deck, checking the cargo and keeping things from breaking. Raul stood on deck watching the horizon but not helping to bail. By the time we reached shore, I was soaked, Cameron and Lily had bruises from being thrown about, and Raul's shirt was dry. The teacher said it was a successful project.' Analyze what the extended analogy imports about each group member's role and experience, and explain why the writer chose this comparison instead of a plain statement like 'I did most of the work.' What does the ship analogy carry that plain words do not?
choices: The analogy imports danger, shared duty, and unequal cost — the storm affects everyone but only some people pay the price, so it shows why the group's success feels unfair to the narrator, which 'I did most of the work' cannot express

The analogy imports that some group members worked harder than others, and a plain statement would communicate the same level of detail about individual effort and contribution since both methods describe who did what

The analogy imports that Raul deliberately avoided his responsibilities and created burden for others, and using a plain statement like 'Raul refused to help' would convey the same accusation about his attitude and choices

The analogy imports that the teacher failed to recognize differences in how much each student contributed, and a plain statement would be a clearer way to communicate this observation about the teacher's evaluation of the project
hints: Map the parts: who is at the helm, who is below deck, who is on deck, what is the shore? What does each person experience in the ship metaphor?
Ask which part of a ship in a storm fits the group project — the danger is shared, the labor is not, and the cost is not. What does 'I did most of the work' lose?

problemText: A story's narrator tells the reader that the school bus already left five minutes early. Jordan, unaware of this, tells his friend, 'Relax, we've got plenty of time before the bus comes.' Based on this, what does dramatic irony require to exist in this moment of the story?
choices: A gap between what the reader knows (the bus left early) and what Jordan knows (he thinks there's still time)
A character who feels afraid even though nothing bad will happen (Jordan panicking about a bus that was never actually late)
A character who says the opposite of what he actually means (Jordan secretly hoping the bus left without him)
A moment where the reader is just as unsure as Jordan about the bus (neither one knowing yet whether it has already left)
hints: Dramatic irony always needs a fact the reader has that the character lacks.
Ask whether Jordan's confident line means something different to him than it does to you.

problemText: The lifeguard chair sat empty because Coach Reyes had gone inside to answer a phone call ten minutes earlier. Mia dove off the diving board and called out to her little cousin, 'Don't worry, the lifeguard's watching us the whole time!' Her cousin adjusted his floaties and grinned, ready to jump in too. Which line delivers the fact that opens the gap between what the reader knows and what Mia knows?
choices: Mia dove off the diving board and called out to her little cousin, laughing as she hit the water with a splash.
The lifeguard chair sat empty because Coach Reyes had gone inside to answer a phone call ten minutes earlier.
Her cousin adjusted his floaties and grinned, ready to jump in too, eager to copy his big cousin's dive.
Don't worry, the lifeguard's watching us the whole time, so nothing bad could possibly happen to us!
hints: Look for the line where the narration leaves Mia and reports something she could not have seen.
The gap opens before Mia speaks, not while she is acting or talking.

problemText: Every window in the house had been decorated with cobwebs and a motion-sensor skeleton for the neighborhood haunted-house contest, and the porch light had been unscrewed on purpose to add an extra scare for visitors. Grandma Ruth, visiting for the first time that fall, told her daughter on the phone that she couldn't wait to see the house 'all lit up and cheerful' when she arrived that night. What effect does this dramatic irony most likely create for the reader?
choices: Suspense, because Grandma Ruth is walking toward a dangerous situation she cannot see coming
Suspense, because the reader has no more information about the house than Grandma Ruth does
Humor, because Grandma Ruth's mistaken expectation will only lead to a startling but harmless surprise
Humor, because Grandma Ruth already knows the house is decorated for Halloween
hints: Ask what Grandma Ruth actually loses when she discovers the truth about the decorations.
Compare a red face or a startle to a real injury or betrayal before choosing suspense or humor.

problemText: The bakery's walk-in freezer had frozen shut that morning after the compressor iced over, though the manager hadn't posted a sign about it yet. Owen, hurrying to grab butter for the morning rush, told the new hire, 'Don't stress, that freezer door practically opens itself.' Which statement correctly identifies the dramatic irony's effect and explains why, based on what closing the gap will cost Owen?
choices: Suspense, because Owen will not learn the truth until he tries the door himself.
Dramatic irony does not apply here, because the reader is only guessing that the freezer is frozen shut.
Suspense, because a frozen freezer could cause a real injury to Owen during the morning rush.
Humor, because the worst outcome is Owen looking foolish tugging at a stuck door, not real harm.
hints: First check whether the passage states the freezer fact as certain, not just something Owen suspects.
Then ask what finding out will actually cost Owen — dignity or real harm.

problemText: The zip line's safety cable had frayed all the way through after last week's storm, though the park hadn't reopened the trail to post a warning sign yet. Eli, feeling nervous but determined to impress his cousins, clipped into the harness and announced, 'This is totally safe, I checked it myself this morning.' Which statement correctly names the effect of the dramatic irony and explains why, based on what closing the gap will cost Eli?
choices: Suspense, because the reader knows the cable is frayed through and Eli is trusting a device that could fail and hurt him.
Suspense, because Eli feels nervous, even though what he is actually walking toward is only mild embarrassment.
Humor, because Eli's nervousness about the harness makes his confident claim funny to the reader.
Humor, because the reader is just as unsure as Eli about whether the cable is actually safe.
hints: Notice that Eli's calm confidence doesn't match the danger the passage already revealed to the reader.
The character's own feelings don't decide the effect — what the gap costs him does.

problemText: A story says that Wyatt thought the substitute teacher seemed unusually strict, and he guessed there might be a pop quiz that day. He tells his friend, 'Bet you anything we have a quiz.' Right now this is only Wyatt's hunch, not dramatic irony, because the reader knows nothing more than he does. Which addition to the passage would turn this into true dramatic irony?
choices: A line stating that Wyatt has always been unusually good at guessing when quizzes are coming, based on his past success
A line stating that the substitute had a stack of quiz papers already printed on her desk before class started
A line stating that the substitute seemed much stricter than the class's regular teacher, which made students nervous
A line stating that Wyatt felt a knot of nervousness in his stomach walking into class, unsure if his guess was right
hints: A hunch becomes dramatic irony only once the story hands the reader a fact the character doesn't have.
Look for an addition where the narration steps away from Wyatt to report something he couldn't have seen.

problemText: A theme develops across a short story in three stages: a before, a turn, and an after. Which statement below correctly describes what the turn is in this pattern?
choices: The final event in the story, occurring after the turn, where the reader can plainly see what the theme is.
The single change in a character or in the setting without which the ending's theme could not happen.
The opening situation before any change occurs, where several different themes are still possible for the story to develop.
The most dramatic or exciting event that occurs somewhere in the middle of the story, even if it changes nothing important.
hints: Think about what sits between the before and the after, not the before or after themselves.
It is defined by what becomes different afterward, not by how exciting it is.

problemText: For weeks, Marcus left his bike unlocked in the driveway overnight, and it was always there in the morning. One night a storm knocked over the neighbor's fence, and the noise woke half the street. The next week, the city installed a streetlight at the end of the driveway, lighting the yard until dawn. After that, Marcus still left the bike unlocked, but now he glanced out his window before bed to check it was still under the light. The theme of this passage is: feeling watched changes how carefully people guard what they already trusted was safe. Which choice correctly names the turn and its kind?
choices: Marcus glancing out his window before bed to check on the bike, a change in a character showing he now feels responsible.
The storm knocking over the neighbor's fence, a change in the setting that made the street pay attention to the driveway.
The streetlight being installed at the end of the driveway, a change in the setting that lets Marcus see the bike from his window.
Marcus leaving his bike unlocked overnight for weeks, a change in a character since he trusted his driveway was safe.
hints: Ask what is different about the driveway itself after the change, not how loud the change was.
One of these choices describes the story's starting situation, which cannot itself be the turn.

problemText: The library reading room had been quiet for years, chairs squeaking, kids passing notes when the librarian looked away. In October the librarian repainted the walls a pale blue. In November she moved the returns desk directly beside the corner table where the loudest kids used to gather, so every conversation there passed a few feet from her desk. By December those kids had spread out to other tables, and the corner was nearly always empty. The theme of this passage is: people change their habits when they can no longer do them unnoticed. Which choice correctly names the turn and its kind?
choices: The kids spreading out to other tables, a change in a character, because it is the moment the theme becomes visible.
Repainting the walls pale blue, a change in the setting, because a new color changes how the room feels to everyone in it.
The chairs squeaking for years, an event, because it happens repeatedly throughout the passage.
Moving the returns desk beside the corner table, a change in the setting, because it removes the kids' ability to talk unnoticed.
hints: A setting change only counts as a turn if it changes what someone can actually do or see there.
One of these choices describes the ending where the theme pays off, not the change that produced it.

problemText: Every Sunday, Grandpa cooked the same stew, and Elena set the table without being asked, though she'd complained about the chore for years. One Sunday, the power went out during a storm, and they ate the stew cold by candlelight, laughing about it. The following month, Grandpa's hands started shaking too badly to hold the ladle, and he asked Elena to stir the pot for the first time. After that, Elena arrived early every Sunday, before Grandpa even asked, to start the stew herself. The theme of this passage is: helping someone by necessity can turn a chore into something you choose. Using the cover test, which change is the turn?
choices: Grandpa asking Elena to stir the pot for the first time because his hands were shaking, a change in a character, since covering it makes Elena's early arrivals afterward unexplained.
The power going out during the storm, a change in the setting, since covering that event would remove the candlelight dinner scene that gives the story its warmth and theme.
Elena arriving early every Sunday to start the stew herself, a change in a character, since covering it removes the final moment when the reader can clearly see what the theme is.
Elena setting the table without being asked for years, a change in a character, since covering it would erase the story's starting point and the routine the theme grows out of.
hints: Try hiding each candidate change and re-reading the last sentence to see if it still makes sense.
The loudest event in a passage often turns out to change nothing about any character.

problemText: The apartment building's laundry room used to have two broken machines out of six, so tenants waited around, chatting while they waited for a free machine. In June, the landlord fixed both broken machines. That same week, a new tenant, Mr. Ortiz, started coming down at exactly nine every night, though nobody had asked him to keep a schedule. By August, the tenants who used to linger and talk were in and out in ten minutes each, since a machine was always free the moment they arrived. The theme of this passage is: convenience can quietly end the conversations that inconvenience used to create. Which choice correctly names the turn and its kind?
choices: Mr. Ortiz coming down at exactly nine every night, a change in a character, because it shows a new routine forming in the laundry room.
The landlord fixing both broken machines, a change in the setting, because tenants no longer have to wait for a free machine and lose the reason to linger.
The tenants being in and out in ten minutes by August, a change in a character, because it is the moment the theme becomes visible to the reader.
The laundry room having two broken machines out of six, a change in the setting, because it explains why tenants used to wait around together.
hints: Check whether each detail actually connects to the reason tenants stopped lingering, not just to timing.
One of these choices describes the starting situation, and a starting situation is not itself a change.

problemText: Coach Reyes required every player to run suicides after a loss, no exceptions, and the team dreaded losses more than the losing itself. In their eighth game, the team lost by one point on a call the referee later admitted was wrong. That night, Coach Reyes posted the referee's apology on the locker room door instead of assigning suicides. Two weeks later, after a lopsided loss with no bad calls involved, Coach Reyes still skipped the suicides, telling the team to just watch the film instead. By the end of the season, players were staying late to watch extra film on their own, without Coach Reyes asking. The theme of this passage is: once punishment stops being about fairness, people start choosing to improve instead of just avoiding pain. Which choice correctly names the turn, using the cover test to rule out the others?
choices: The referee's wrong call in the eighth game, an event, because it is the most dramatic moment but by itself does not establish that punishment stopped being about fairness.

Coach Reyes posting the referee's apology instead of assigning suicides after the bad call, a change in a character, because it could still be explained as a fairness correction rather than a real change in his rule.

Coach Reyes skipping suicides after a lopsided loss with no bad call and telling the team to watch film, a change in a character, because it removes fairness as the reason and the theme cannot happen without it.
Players staying late to watch extra film without being asked, a change in a character, because it is where the theme becomes visible in the story.
hints: Ask whether the first skipped punishment could still be explained by fairness alone, since the referee really was wrong that time.
The turn must be the point after which the ending cannot be explained any other way.

problemText: A student reads two stories and says, 'Both of these have a wizard in them, so they must share a pattern.' Using the idea that a pattern is the bones of a story and not its costume, evaluate whether the student's reasoning is sound.
choices: The student is right, since any figure who appears often across many different old stories, such as a wizard, always signals that two stories automatically share the same pattern of events.
The student is right, since sharing one striking character, such as a wizard who casts spells, is exactly what makes two different stories share the same underlying pattern of events.
A wizard is a costume detail, not a pattern; the two stories only share a pattern if stripping out the names and setting leaves the same one-sentence shape of events.
A wizard could count as a pattern only if that wizard always sets exactly three trials for the hero, since three trials is claimed to be the one shape every wizard belongs to.
hints: Think about what it means to 'strip the clothes' off a story before comparing it to another.
A dragon was described as a costume a story can wear without any old shape underneath; ask whether a wizard is any different.

problemText: Read this excerpt: 'The lifeguard had told the twins twice not to swim past the yellow buoys because of the current. Marco swam past them anyway to retrieve a beach ball, and thirty feet out the current caught him and pulled him toward the rocks before the lifeguard managed to reach him.' Which pattern from old stories does this excerpt draw on?
choices: The humble helper: Marco is the overlooked member of the group whose swim past the buoys ends up saving the beach ball for everyone else.
The three trials: Marco has to complete increasingly difficult swims past the buoys, each harder than the last, before the lifeguard will let him retrieve the ball.
The trickster outwitted: Marco tries to fool the lifeguard into looking away so he can retrieve the ball, and the current outsmarts him instead.
The warning ignored: Marco was told plainly not to swim past the buoys, did it anyway, and the current pulling him toward the rocks is the warned-about danger coming true.
hints: Look for whether a character was told plainly not to do something beforehand.
Check whether the ending matches the thing warned about, rather than a series of tests or a trick.

problemText: Read this excerpt: 'Nora had a reputation for winning every board game by quietly changing the rules mid-play when nobody was looking. During the tournament final, she tried to slip an extra move past her opponent, a quiet freshman named Theo who rarely spoke. Theo said nothing, but he had been recording the whole game on his phone the entire time, and when he showed the video to the judges, Nora's win was reversed and Theo advanced instead.' Which pattern from old stories does this excerpt draw on?
choices: The trickster outwitted: Nora, who lives by bending the rules unnoticed, is beaten by Theo, the quiet opponent she had not taken seriously.
The humble helper: Theo is the least regarded member of the tournament whose recording decides the outcome for someone else on his team.
The warning ignored: Nora was told plainly not to change the rules, did it anyway, and losing the final is the warned-about outcome coming true.
The three trials: Nora must pass three increasingly difficult rounds against Theo before the judges will award her the win.
hints: Ask whether the outcome lands on the character's own account or benefits someone else instead.
Nora is the character who habitually bends rules to win unnoticed by others.

problemText: In an old family story, a queen who wanted rain had to ask the sky three times, each time in harder weather than the last, and the rain came only after the third asking. In Mia's telling: 'The school board president needed the town council's approval for a new track three times: first at a regular meeting, then at a snowed-in special session nobody expected her to reach, and finally during a power outage, where she pitched her plan by flashlight to a room that had already decided to vote no. They approved it unanimously right after she finished.' Which choice best explains how this modern telling renders the three-trials pattern new?
choices: Reversed outcome: the pattern promises success on the third trial, but the council actually rejects her proposal despite her effort during the outage.
Changed setting: the three escalating trials and the win on the third are both kept, and only the place and details, council meetings instead of pleas to the sky, are new.
Swapped role: the council members take on the role of the young hero who must pass trials, while Mia's president becomes the powerful figure judging them.
Warning ignored: the president was told plainly not to pursue the track expansion, pursued it anyway, and the council's approval is the danger she was warned about coming true.
hints: Check whether the ending the pattern promises, success on the third try, actually happens in Mia's telling.
Check whether the president and the council are playing the usual kinds of roles, the one who wants something and the one with the power to grant it.

problemText: Read this excerpt: 'Every year at the county fair, the six-year-olds among the exhibitors are barely noticed next to the seniors' prize hogs and quilts. This year, when the ribbon judges' scale broke down five minutes before the pie contest results were due, it was Emmy, the fair's youngest baker at seven years old, who remembered her grandmother kept a spare kitchen scale in her truck, ran to get it, and got the judging finished on time. The blue ribbon that day went to a teenager's pie, and nobody but the judges ever learned whose scale had made the contest possible.' Which choice correctly identifies the pattern this excerpt draws on and how the modern telling treats it?
choices: It draws on the trickster outwitted pattern, but swaps the role: Emmy fools the judges into believing she is helpful, when she actually wants the ribbon prize for herself alone.
It draws on the humble helper pattern, but reverses the outcome: Emmy's help fails to matter, since the ribbon goes to the teenager instead of rewarding her for helping.
It draws on the humble helper pattern, and it keeps the pattern exactly: the overlooked youngest exhibitor's help decides the outcome for someone else, the teenager who wins the ribbon.
It draws on the three trials pattern, with a changed setting: Emmy must pass three increasingly difficult tasks with the borrowed scale before the judges can award any ribbon.
hints: Recall that the humble helper's promised ending is that the help lands on someone else, not on the helper.
Decide which character type and pattern actually fits before deciding whether any move has changed it.

problemText: Read this excerpt: 'Toby ran a rumor mill at school, spinning stories about kids he considered easy targets to get out of trouble himself. When a rumor he started about a substitute teacher got the sub in trouble with the office, nobody ever found out it was Toby, and he moved on to a new rumor the next week without a second thought.' Does this excerpt draw on the trickster-outwitted pattern from old stories, and if so, how does the modern telling treat it?
choices: No, because a trickster fooling other people is just a costume detail like a dragon, and nothing in the excerpt actually shows any of the traditional trickster story shapes being used.
No, because the trickster pattern only ever applies when the person being fooled holds real power, like a king or a queen, and Toby only ever fools a substitute teacher.
Yes, with a changed setting: the bones and the promised ending are both kept exactly, and only the location, a school hallway instead of a village or forest, has changed.
Yes, with a reversed outcome: Toby is the trickster character type, and the pattern's promised ending, being outwitted, never arrives, since he gets away with the rumor completely.
hints: Recall that getting away with it is explicitly one of the ways a pattern can be rendered new.
Ask whether the promised ending for a trickster, being fooled in turn, actually shows up anywhere in the excerpt.
